once.soru: In what form does a plant store the extra food it makes by photosynthesis?

secenekler.neden: Glucose molecules join to form starch. Potatoes and wheat are examples of this store.
Glycogen is the storage substance of animals and fungi.
Cellulose is not a storage substance. It is the building material of the cell wall.

cards.p: Plants living on land faced the problems of drying out, moving water and reproducing. The cuticle reduced water loss, stomata controlled gas exchange and vascular bundles carried water. Pollen and seeds freed reproduction from depending on water.

ogeler: A fern has vascular bundles, but no seeds. It reproduces with spores.
A pine is a gymnosperm. Its seed sits exposed on a cone scale.

cards.p: Mosses and liverworts have no vascular bundles and no true roots, stems or leaves. They hold on with rhizoids and stay short. Their sperm reach the egg by swimming through water, so they live in damp places.

cards.key: Rhizoids mainly serve to anchor the plant. A moss absorbs water through its whole surface. Mosses, together with lichens, are among the pioneer species that first settle on bare rock.

once.soru: Why do mosses mostly live in damp, shady places?

secenekler.neden: For fertilization, the sperm must swim through water to the egg. Also, a moss has no vascular bundles to carry water.
Mosses carry out photosynthesis, so they need light.
Mosses have no true roots. They hold on with rhizoids.

cards.p: Ferns, horsetails and club mosses have xylem and phloem. They form true roots, stems and leaves. However, these plants have no seeds or flowers. They reproduce with spores.

A fern has no seeds.
These are the plant's normal reproductive structures.

cards.h: Alternation of generations: gametophyte and sporophyte
cards.p: A 2n cell has two of each chromosome, and an n cell has one. In alternation of generations, the 2n sporophyte makes spores by meiosis. A spore grows into the n gametophyte, and the gametophyte makes gametes.

cards.h: How did the dominant generation change?
cards.p: As you just saw, the gametophyte is dominant in mosses and the sporophyte is dominant in ferns. In seed plants, the gametophyte stays microscopic. Pollen is the male gametophyte, and the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

cards.p: In seed plants, pollen is carried by wind or animals, so fertilization does not depend on water. A seed is made of an embryo, stored food and a coat. It can wait through drought and sprouts when conditions are right.

cards.key: A spore is a single cell. A seed is a multicellular structure made of an embryo, stored food and a coat.

once.soru: What advantage does a seed have over a spore?

secenekler.neden: A seed holds an embryo, a store of food to nourish it and a protective coat. A spore is a single cell.
A spore is a single cell, so it is much lighter than a seed.
A spore forms by meiosis, while a seed develops after fertilization.

cards.p: Pine, spruce, fir and juniper are gymnosperms. Their seeds sit exposed on cone scales. These plants have no flowers or fruits, and their pollen is carried by the wind. Most stay green all year.

cards.p: In angiosperms, the ovule is protected inside the ovary, and the ovary becomes the fruit. Double fertilization happens only in this group. One sperm forms the zygote, and the other forms the endosperm, the food tissue in the seed.

once.soru: Which part of the flower does a cherry fruit develop from?

secenekler.neden: After fertilization, the ovary becomes the fruit, and the ovule inside it becomes the seed.
The petals fall off after fertilization.
Pollen is the male gametophyte, and it does not become a fruit.

cards.h: Monocots and dicots: stems and leaves
cards.p: Angiosperms are divided by their number of cotyledons, or seed leaves. In monocots, leaf veins are parallel and vascular bundles are scattered. In dicots, veins form a network, bundles are arranged in a ring and there is a cambium.

once.soru: A plant has leaves with parallel veins. Which group is it in?

secenekler.neden: Parallel veins are a sign of monocots. Wheat, corn and tulips are examples.
In dicots, the veins form a network.
The cotyledon split is used only for angiosperms.

cards.h: Monocots and dicots: roots and flowers
cards.p: Monocots have fibrous roots, and their flower parts come in multiples of 3. Wheat and tulips are examples. Dicots have a taproot, and their flower parts come in multiples of 4 or 5. Beans and roses are examples. To identify a plant, look at several features together.

cards.p: Plants are the producers on land. They release oxygen and take up CO2. Their roots prevent erosion. They give people food, timber, fiber and medicine. Coal also formed from ancient plant forests.

once.soru: When the trees on a slope are cut down, which problem gets worse?

secenekler.neden: Roots hold the soil. When the trees are cut down, rain washes the soil away.
Plant cover does not affect earthquakes.
Other gases cause the thinning of the ozone layer.

cards.p:
• Plants are eukaryotic, multicellular, have cellulose walls and protect an embryo.
• Mosses are nonvascular and seedless. Ferns are vascular, but seedless.
• The gametophyte is dominant in mosses, and the sporophyte in all other plants.
• In gymnosperms the seed is exposed, and in angiosperms it is inside a fruit.
• Monocots have parallel veins and fibrous roots.

quiz.q: Put the life cycle of a fern in order, starting with the sporophyte.
ogeler: The sporophyte (2n) makes spores (n) by meiosis
The spore grows by mitosis and forms the gametophyte (prothallus)
The gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis
The gametes fuse and form a zygote (2n)
The zygote grows and forms a new sporophyte
quiz.e: The sporophyte makes haploid spores by meiosis, and a spore grows by mitosis into the gametophyte. The gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis. The diploid zygote formed by fertilization grows into a sporophyte again.

quiz.q: Sort each feature into monocot or dicot.
quiz.e: In monocots, veins are parallel, bundles are scattered, roots are fibrous and flower parts come in multiples of 3. In dicots, veins form a network, bundles are arranged in a ring and there is a taproot. Their embryos have two cotyledons.

quiz.q: The cells of a moss's green, leafy plant have 10 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in the cells of this moss's sporophyte?
quiz.e: The green plant we see in a moss is the gametophyte, and n = 10. The sporophyte grows from the zygote formed when two gametes fuse. That is why it has 2n = 20 chromosomes.

quiz.q: What is the main feature that sets a pine apart from an apple tree?
o: The apple's seed is inside a fruit, and the pine's is exposed.
The pine reproduces by spores, and the apple by seeds.
The apple has vascular bundles, and the pine does not.
The pine does not photosynthesize, and the apple does.
quiz.e: Both are vascular seed plants. The difference lies in how the seed is protected. A pine is a gymnosperm and has no flowers or fruit. An apple tree is an angiosperm.
y: A pine also reproduces by seeds. The difference is whether the seed is inside a fruit or exposed.
A pine is also a vascular plant. The main difference is whether the seed is enclosed in a fruit.
A pine has green leaves and carries out photosynthesis. The difference is whether the seed is exposed or enclosed.

bitki-biyolojisi.title: Plant biology
bitki-biyolojisi.summary: Plant tissues, how water and food are transported, plant hormones and reproduction

cards.p: The root anchors the plant in the soil and absorbs water and minerals. The root cap protects the tip of the root, and root hairs enlarge the absorbing surface. The stem holds the leaves up toward the light and transports substances.

once.soru: Which organ is the potato tuber we eat?

secenekler.neden: The eyes on a potato are buds, and buds are found on stems.
A carrot is a root, but a potato tuber is an underground stem.
A tuber is not a leaf. It is a stem that stores food.

cards.p: The waxy cuticle reduces water loss. The tightly packed palisade mesophyll carries out most of the photosynthesis. The loosely packed spongy mesophyll makes gas exchange easier. Stomata are mostly on the underside of the leaf.

etk.soru: Tap the numbers on the leaf section and see what each layer does.

noktalar.acik: The cuticle is a waterproof, waxy layer. It reduces water loss from the leaf.
The upper epidermis is a single row of clear cells. It lets light in and protects the tissues below.
The palisade mesophyll is made of tightly packed cells rich in chloroplasts. Most of the photosynthesis happens here.
The cells of the spongy mesophyll are loosely packed. The air spaces between them make gas exchange easier.
This is a leaf vein. The xylem on top brings water and minerals, and the phloem below carries away the sugar that is made.
The lower epidermis covers the underside of the leaf. In most plants, most of the stomata are here.
A stoma is the opening between two guard cells. CO<sub>2</sub> enters here, and O<sub>2</sub> and water vapor leave.

once.soru: In which layer of a leaf does most of the photosynthesis happen?

secenekler.neden: The palisade mesophyll has tightly packed cells rich in chloroplasts.
Epidermal cells usually have no chloroplasts.
The cuticle is not a layer of cells. It is a waxy covering.

cards.p: A tissue made of cells that can divide is called a meristem. The apical meristem makes the plant grow taller. The cambium makes the stem thicker by producing xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside. In seasonal climates, one annual ring forms each year.

cards.key: The bark of old stems is cork tissue made of dead cells. Flax and hemp fibers are sclerenchyma.

once.soru: Which tissue makes a walnut shell hard?

secenekler.neden: Sclerenchyma is made of cells that are hardened with lignin and mostly dead.
Parenchyma cells are alive and thin-walled.
Collenchyma is a living, flexible tissue. It is not hard.

cards.p: Xylem carries water and minerals from the root to the leaves. Its conducting cells are dead when mature. Phloem carries organic substances. Its sieve tube cells are alive, and the flow can go in both directions.

cards.key: Xylem cells are dead and carry water upward. Phloem cells are alive and can carry food in both directions.

etk.soru: Does each feature belong to xylem or phloem?
ogeler: In phloem, food flows from source to sink. The sink can be in the root or at a growing tip.

once.soru: Which tissue carries sugar from the leaf to the root?

secenekler.neden: Phloem carries organic substances from source to sink.
Xylem carries water and minerals upward.
The epidermis is a protective tissue. It does not transport anything.

cards.p: The root loads minerals into the xylem by active transport. Water follows by osmosis, and root pressure builds up. On humid nights, water drips from the edges of leaves. This is called guttation. However, root pressure is not enough to lift water to the top of tall trees.

once.soru: What causes the water drops seen on the edges of some leaves in the morning?

secenekler.neden: At night, when transpiration slows, root pressure pushes water out through the leaf edges. This is called guttation.
In transpiration, water leaves as vapor and no drops form.
The drops come from inside the leaf, out of pores along the edges.

cards.p: The evaporation of water through the stomata is called transpiration. During transpiration, water in the xylem is pulled upward. Water molecules cling both to each other (cohesion) and to the vessel walls (adhesion). This lets the column of water rise without breaking.

cards.p: A stoma is the opening between two guard cells. In light, K+ ions enter the guard cells, and water follows them. As the cells swell, the stoma opens. In the dark or during drought, the stoma closes.

cards.p: In phloem, food flows from a source, such as a mature leaf, to a sink, such as a root, a fruit or a growing tip. At the source, sugar is loaded, water enters and pressure rises. At the sink, pressure drops. This is called the pressure flow model.

cards.p: Hormones control growth in very small amounts. Auxin suppresses side buds. This is called apical dominance. Cytokinin stimulates cell division, and gibberellin stimulates elongation. Abscisic acid closes the stomata, and ethylene ripens fruit.

cards.p: A plant growing in response to the direction of a stimulus is called a tropism. The stem grows toward light, and the root grows toward gravity and water. A nastic movement does not depend on the direction of the stimulus. A sensitive plant folding up when touched is an example.

once.soru: A bee carries pollen from one flower and drops it on the stigma of another flower. What is this called?

secenekler.neden: Carrying pollen to the stigma is called pollination. Fertilization happens later.
Fertilization is the joining of sperm and egg, and it happens after the pollen tube grows.
Germination is when a seed starts to grow.

cards.p: After fertilization, the ovule becomes the seed, and the ovary becomes the fruit. A seed needs water, a suitable temperature and oxygen to germinate. Some seeds also need light.

cards.p:
• The apical meristem makes a plant grow taller, and the cambium makes it grow thicker.
• Xylem carries water upward, and phloem carries food in both directions.
• Water rises by transpiration pull and root pressure. Light and K+ open the stomata.
• Hormones control growth and tropisms.
• In double fertilization, the zygote is 2n and the endosperm is 3n.

quiz.q: The root cells of a plant have 2n = 14 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in this plant's endosperm cells?
quiz.e: The endosperm forms when one sperm (n = 7) joins two polar nuclei (7 + 7). That is why it carries 3n = 21 chromosomes.

quiz.q: Match each plant hormone with its main effect.
quiz.e: Auxin suppresses side buds, and cytokinin stimulates cell division. Gibberellin lengthens the stem and starts germination. Abscisic acid closes the stomata during drought. Ethylene, a gas, ripens fruit.

quiz.q: Match each plant movement with its name.
quiz.e: Turning toward light is phototropism, growing in response to gravity is gravitropism and winding around a support is thigmotropism. A sensitive plant folding up does not depend on the direction of the stimulus and happens through turgor. It is a nastic movement.

quiz.q: On the morning after a humid night, water drops appear only at the tips along a plant's leaf edges, and the drops contain minerals. What causes the drops?
o: A big increase in transpiration
Stomata staying open at night
Water vapor in the air condensing (dew)
Root pressure pushing water through water pores
quiz.e: This is called guttation. When transpiration is low, root pressure pushes mineral-rich water from the xylem out through the water pores along the leaf edge. Dew forms on every surface and contains no minerals.
y: In transpiration, water leaves as vapor, and transpiration slows in humid night air. The drops are caused by root pressure.
The water leaving the stomata is vapor. The drops that contain minerals are pushed out through water pores by root pressure.
Dew forms on the whole surface and contains no minerals. Drops seen only at the edge tips are guttation.

sinir-sistemi.title: Nervous system
sinir-sistemi.summary: Neurons, impulses, synapses, the brain, the spinal cord and the autonomic nervous system

cards.p: A nerve cell is called a neuron. Its short, branched extensions are called dendrites, and its single long extension is called the axon. A fatty myelin sheath wraps and insulates the axon. The gaps in the sheath are called nodes of Ranvier.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the neuron.

noktalar.acik: Dendrites are short, branched extensions that come out of the cell body.
The cell body holds the nucleus and most of the organelles. It runs the neuron's life processes.
The axon is the single long extension that comes out of the cell body.
Myelin is a fatty, insulating sheath that wraps the axon. It speeds up conduction.
A node of Ranvier is a gap in the myelin. The impulse jumps from node to node.
The axon terminal is the branching end of the axon. Its vesicles carry neurotransmitters.

cards.h: Types of neurons and glial cells
cards.p: A sensory neuron carries a stimulus to the central nervous system. An interneuron processes the information. A motor neuron carries the command to a muscle or gland. Glial cells support the neurons.

cards.key: Glial cells feed and protect neurons and make the myelin sheath. Mature neurons usually do not divide, but glial cells can.

once.soru: Which neuron carries the "contract" command to a muscle in your arm?

secenekler.neden: A motor neuron carries the command to a muscle or gland.
A sensory neuron carries the stimulus to the center.
An interneuron processes information in the brain and spinal cord.

once.soru: Does a resting neuron use ATP?

secenekler.neden: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump works nonstop and uses ATP.
The pump also works at rest. The ion flows during a stimulus do not use ATP.
The pump uses one ATP per cycle.

cards.p: When a stimulus passes the threshold, Na⁺ ions enter the cell and the inside of the membrane becomes positive. This is called depolarization. Then K⁺ ions leave and the inside becomes negative again. This is called repolarization. These ion flows do not use ATP.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><line x1='40' y1='25' x2='40' y2='178' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='178' x2='308' y2='178' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='77' x2='305' y2='77' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><line x1='40' y1='141' x2='305' y2='141' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M40,158 L120,158 Q132,156 140,141 L163,45 Q170,32 177,45 L195,158 Q202,172 215,166 Q230,159 245,158 L305,158' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><g font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'><text x='35' y='45'>+30</text><text x='35' y='81'>0</text><text x='35' y='162'>−70</text><text x='35' y='20'>mV</text></g><g font-size='11' text-anchor='end'><text x='144' y='95' fill='var(--c4)'>depolarization</text><text x='144' y='109' fill='var(--c4)'>Na⁺ enters</text></g><g font-size='11'><text x='192' y='100' fill='var(--c3)'>repolarization</text><text x='192' y='114' fill='var(--c3)'>K⁺ leaves</text></g><text x='305' y='135' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>threshold ≈ −55</text><text x='48' y='152' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>rest</text><text x='305' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>time (≈ a few ms)</text></svg>
cards.key: The ions pass through channels by diffusion. The pump then moves them back to where they were.

cards.p: A stimulus below the threshold does not create an impulse. When the stimulus reaches the threshold, a full-size impulse forms. A stronger stimulus does not make the impulse bigger. It only raises the frequency of impulses. This is called the all-or-none rule.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='10' y='20' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>response (impulse)</text><g fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'><line x1='20' y1='85' x2='90' y2='85'/><path d='M125,85 L150,85 L160,35 L170,85 L195,85'/><path d='M230,85 L255,85 L265,35 L275,85 L300,85'/></g><text x='55' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>no impulse</text><text x='10' y='108' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>stimulus</text><line x1='20' y1='160' x2='300' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)'/><g fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--c4)'><rect x='45' y='140' width='20' height='20'/><rect x='150' y='120' width='20' height='40'/><rect x='255' y='100' width='20' height='60'/></g><line x1='20' y1='120' x2='282' y2='120' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='312' y='124' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>threshold</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='55' y='178'>below threshold</text><text x='160' y='178'>threshold value</text><text x='265' y='178'>stronger</text></g><text x='212' y='28' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>same size</text></svg>
cards.key: This rule applies to a single neuron. A nerve, which is a bundle of neurons, responds to a strong stimulus with more neurons.

cards.p: Because myelin is an insulator, ions flow only at the nodes of Ranvier. The impulse jumps from node to node. This speeds up conduction and uses less energy. Conduction is also fast in thick axons.

cards.key: In MS, the myelin sheath breaks down. As a result, conduction slows or stops.

cards.p: The junction between two cells is called a synapse. The axon terminal releases a neurotransmitter into the gap, and it binds to the next cell. Because vesicles are found only in the axon terminal, transmission is one-way.

cards.key: Acetylcholine plays a role in muscle contraction, dopamine in movement and reward, and serotonin in mood. Conduction inside a neuron is electrical, and at most synapses it is chemical.

cards.p: The largest part of the brain is the cerebrum, and the corpus callosum connects its two hemispheres. Thinking, memory, speech and voluntary movement are controlled here.

cards.key: The outer cortex of the cerebrum is gray matter. Vision is handled in the occipital lobe and hearing in the temporal lobe. Voluntary movement starts in the frontal lobe.

once.soru: If the left hemisphere of someone's brain is damaged, on which side does paralysis usually appear?

secenekler.neden: Each hemisphere usually controls the opposite side of the body.
The nerve pathways cross over. So the left hemisphere controls the right side.
One hemisphere mostly controls only one side of the body.

cards.p: The cerebellum keeps balance and coordinates movement. The thalamus relays every sense except smell to the cerebral cortex. The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='sin-11' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><rect x='10' y='14' width='300' height='40' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='24' y='39' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='700'>cerebellum</text><text x='120' y='39' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>balance and muscle coordination</text><rect x='10' y='64' width='300' height='86' rx='6' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='24' y='82' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>diencephalon</text><text x='24' y='108' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='700'>thalamus</text><text x='120' y='108' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>relays senses to the cortex</text><text x='24' y='136' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='700'>hypothalamus</text><text x='120' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>temperature, water, hunger</text><line x1='60' y1='154' x2='60' y2='184' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#sin-11)'/><text x='74' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--c4)'>controls the pituitary (hormone link)</text></svg>
cards.key: The thalamus and hypothalamus are in the diencephalon. By controlling the pituitary, the hypothalamus links the nervous system to hormones. Damage to the cerebellum does not cause paralysis.

once.soru: A person who has been drinking cannot walk straight. Which part is mainly affected?

secenekler.neden: Balance and movement coordination are controlled by the cerebellum.
The medulla controls heartbeat and breathing.
The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst.

cards.p: The brainstem is made of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla, and it connects the brain to the spinal cord. The medulla controls heartbeat, breathing, swallowing and coughing.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='sin-12' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='36' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='22' y='33' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='700'>midbrain</text><text x='112' y='33' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>eye and ear reflexes</text><rect x='10' y='52' width='300' height='36' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='22' y='75' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='700'>pons</text><text x='112' y='75' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>links cerebrum and cerebellum</text><rect x='10' y='94' width='300' height='36' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='22' y='117' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='700'>medulla</text><text x='112' y='117' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>heartbeat, breathing, swallowing</text><line x1='160' y1='134' x2='160' y2='156' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#sin-12)'/><text x='160' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>joins the spinal cord</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla</text></svg>
cards.key: The midbrain controls eye and ear reflexes. The pons links the cerebrum and the cerebellum. Damage to the medulla is directly life-threatening.

once.soru: Where is the center that controls heartbeat and breathing?

secenekler.neden: The heart and breathing centers are in the medulla, in the brainstem.
The cerebrum controls voluntary actions, but the heartbeat is involuntary.
The cerebellum keeps balance and coordinates movement.

cards.h: The spinal cord and the reflex arc
cards.p: The spinal cord is the pathway between the brain and the body, and it is also a reflex center. In a reflex arc, the signal goes from the receptor to a sensory neuron, an interneuron, a motor neuron and the effector, in that order.

cards.key: In the spinal cord, gray matter is inside and white matter is outside. The knee-jerk reflex has no interneuron. The sensory neuron enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root, and the motor neuron leaves through the ventral root.

cards.p: The skull protects the brain, and the vertebrae protect the spinal cord. Three meninges wrap them: the dura mater, the arachnoid and the pia mater. The cerebrospinal fluid between the membranes cushions blows.

once.soru: What is inflammation of the meninges called?

secenekler.neden: Inflammation of the meninges is called meningitis.
In epilepsy, neurons fire in an irregular and excessive way.
Paralysis is the loss of movement in a part of the body.

cards.p: The nerves outside the brain and spinal cord make up the peripheral nervous system. The somatic division controls the skeletal muscles. The autonomic division controls the heart, smooth muscles and glands involuntarily.

text-anchor='middle'><text x='60' y='90'>brain + spinal cord</text><text x='130' y='136'>skeletal muscles</text></g><text x='10' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>autonomic: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, glands, involuntary</text></svg>
cards.key: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The knee-jerk reflex is involuntary, but it is somatic because it uses a skeletal muscle.

once.soru: You cannot stop your heartbeat at will. Which division controls the heart?

secenekler.neden: The autonomic division controls the heart, smooth muscles and glands involuntarily.
The somatic division controls the skeletal muscles.
The cerebrum controls voluntary actions.

cards.p: Most internal organs receive nerves from two separate branches, and their effects are opposite. The sympathetic system prepares the body for action. The parasympathetic system brings the body back to normal at rest and supports digestion.

cards.p: In Alzheimer's disease, neurons are lost. In Parkinson's disease, the neurons that make dopamine decline. In MS, the myelin sheath breaks down. In epilepsy, neurons fire excessively.

cards.key: In Alzheimer's, memory weakens. In MS, the immune system attacks myelin. Alcohol, nicotine and drugs affect synapses. In addiction, more and more of the substance is needed for the same effect.

once.soru: In Parkinson's disease, the neurons that make which substance decline?

secenekler.neden: The dopamine-making neurons in the midbrain decline. This causes tremor and slow movement.
Serotonin is mostly linked to mood.
Acetylcholine works in muscle contraction. The substance that declines in Parkinson's is dopamine.

cards.p:
• In a neuron, the impulse goes from the dendrite to the cell body and then to the axon. Myelin speeds up conduction.
• At rest, the outside of the membrane is positive and the inside is negative. When stimulated, Na⁺ enters first, then K⁺ leaves.
• Transmission at a synapse is chemical and one-way.
• The central nervous system is made of the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral system is divided into somatic and autonomic divisions.

quiz.q: Sort each effect by the autonomic branch that causes it.
quiz.e: The sympathetic system prepares the body for action. It speeds up the heart, dilates the pupil, widens the bronchi and reduces saliva. The parasympathetic system does the opposite at rest and speeds up digestion.

quiz.q: Match each part of the brain with its job.
quiz.e: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, and the medulla controls heartbeat and breathing. The hypothalamus regulates body temperature and water balance, and the thalamus relays the senses to the cerebral cortex. Thinking, memory and speech are controlled by the cerebrum.

quiz.q: Put each structure in the division it belongs to.
quiz.e: The central nervous system is made of the brain and spinal cord. The brain includes the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the brainstem. The nerves outside these make up the peripheral nervous system. The peripheral system is made of the somatic division and the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches of the autonomic division.

quiz.q: On an action potential graph, what happens in the phase where the membrane potential rises quickly from −55 mV to +30 mV?
o: Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ enters the cell.
K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves the cell.
The Na⁺-K⁺ pump uses ATP to bring Na⁺ in.
The membrane closes to all ions and the charge rises by itself.
quiz.e: The rising phase is depolarization. Na⁺ ions enter by diffusion and the inside of the membrane becomes positive. K⁺ leaves during repolarization, when the potential falls.
y: K⁺ leaving causes repolarization and lowers the potential. The fast rise comes from Na⁺ entering.
The Na⁺-K⁺ pump moves Na⁺ ions out and works slowly. The fast rise comes from Na⁺ channels opening.
The membrane potential does not change without ion movement. The rise is caused by Na⁺ ions entering through channels.

endokrin.title: Endocrine system
endokrin.summary: Hormones, endocrine glands and how the body is regulated by chemical signals

cards.p: A hormone is a chemical messenger that a gland releases directly into the blood. Endocrine glands have no ducts. Exocrine glands release their secretions through a duct. Mixed glands do both.

once.soru: A sweat gland releases its secretion onto the skin through a duct. What kind of gland is it?

secenekler.neden: A gland that releases its secretion onto a body surface through a duct is an exocrine gland.
An endocrine gland has no duct, and its secretion goes directly into the blood.
A mixed gland releases secretions both into the blood and into a duct. A sweat gland releases only into a duct.

cards.h: What all hormones have in common
cards.p: A hormone travels through the whole body in the blood, but it only affects target cells that have the right receptor. Even a tiny amount is enough. Hormones are broken down in the liver and removed by the kidneys.

cards.p: Hormones fall into three groups by structure. Insulin and ADH are proteins or peptides, adrenaline and thyroxine are amines, and cortisol and the sex hormones are steroids. Steroids pass through the membrane, and their receptors are inside the cell.

once.soru: Steroid hormones are made from cholesterol. Can they pass easily through the cell membrane?

secenekler.neden: Steroids are fat-soluble. So they pass directly through the lipid layer of the membrane.
The ones that cannot pass through the membrane are protein hormones, and their receptors are on the membrane.
Steroids cross the membrane without needing a carrier.

cards.p: The nervous system sends messages through neurons. This is fast, short-lived and goes to a specific target. The endocrine system sends messages through the blood. This is slow, long-lasting and affects a wide area. The hypothalamus links the two systems.

cards.h: The hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary
cards.p: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary. ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary and released into the blood from there. ADH increases water reabsorption in the kidneys. Oxytocin contracts the uterus during childbirth.

once.soru: You lost a lot of water and you are thirsty. How do your kidneys adjust your urine?

secenekler.neden: ADH rises and the kidney reabsorbs water. So urine becomes less and darker.
This happens when the body has too much water.
The kidney constantly adjusts urine to the body's water balance.

cards.h: The anterior pituitary: manager of the glands
cards.p: The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones. GH drives growth. TSH stimulates the thyroid, ACTH the adrenal cortex, and FSH and LH the sex glands. Prolactin drives milk production.

once.soru: The anterior pituitary also controls other glands. If it is damaged, what happens to the thyroid?

secenekler.neden: The TSH that stimulates the thyroid stops coming, and thyroxine falls.
When its signal stops, a gland does not speed up. It slows down.
The thyroid works on the TSH released by the anterior pituitary.

cards.p: The thyroid releases the hormone thyroxine, which contains iodine, and thyroxine sets the metabolic rate. If there is not enough iodine, the gland grows. This is called a goiter. Using iodized salt prevents goiter.

cards.p: The parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone. When blood Ca2+ falls, parathyroid hormone releases calcium from bone. When Ca2+ rises, the thyroid releases calcitonin, which sends calcium into bone.

once.soru: Blood calcium has dropped. What happens to the calcium in the bones?

secenekler.neden: Parathyroid hormone releases calcium from bone, and blood calcium rises.
Calcium is sent into bone by calcitonin when blood levels are high.
Bone is the body's calcium store, and this store is used when calcium levels fall.

cards.p: The cortex of the adrenal gland releases cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol raises blood sugar under stress, and aldosterone makes the body hold on to Na+ and water. The medulla of the gland releases adrenaline.

cards.key: The adrenal medulla is stimulated by sympathetic nerves. Adrenaline is the response to sudden danger, and cortisol is the response to long-lasting stress.

once.soru: You hear a noise in the dark at night, you jump and your heart races. Which hormone causes this?

secenekler.neden: In sudden danger, the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and the heart speeds up.
Insulin lowers blood sugar. It does not speed up the heart.
Melatonin sets the sleep cycle.

cards.p: The endocrine part of the pancreas is called the islets of Langerhans. After a meal, β cells release insulin and blood sugar falls. When you are hungry, α cells release glucagon and blood sugar rises.

cards.key: Insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood sugar. Glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise it. The liver and muscles store glucose as glycogen.

cards.p: If insulin is missing or does not work, blood sugar rises and sugar passes into the urine. This is called diabetes. In type 1 diabetes, the β cells are destroyed. In type 2 diabetes, cells do not respond to insulin.

once.soru: A patient's pancreas cannot make insulin. What happens to their blood sugar?

secenekler.neden: Without insulin, cells cannot take in glucose, so glucose stays in the blood.
The hormone that lowers blood sugar is insulin. Without insulin, sugar does not fall.
There is no other hormone that lowers blood sugar.

cards.h: Sex glands, the pineal gland and the thymus
cards.p: The testes release testosterone, and the ovaries release estrogen and progesterone. The pineal gland releases melatonin in the dark and sets the sleep cycle. T lymphocytes mature in the thymus.

once.soru: You look at a bright screen for a long time before bed. Why is your sleep delayed?

secenekler.neden: Melatonin rises in the dark, and screen light suppresses it.
Insulin regulates blood sugar, not sleep.
A drop in adrenaline makes falling asleep easier, not harder.

cards.p: In childhood, too much GH causes gigantism and too little causes dwarfism. In adults, too much GH causes acromegaly. A lack of thyroxine causes congenital hypothyroidism, and a lack of ADH causes diabetes insipidus.

etk.soru: Match each disorder with its cause.
ciftler: Too much GH in an adult

once.soru: If an adult has too much GH, do they grow taller?

secenekler.neden: In adults the growth plates have closed. So the hands, feet and jaw get thicker instead.
Height increases only while the growth plates are open, that is, in childhood.
After the growth plates close, height does not increase at all.

cards.p: The stomach increases acid secretion with the hormone gastrin. The small intestine triggers bicarbonate release with the hormone secretin. An empty stomach releases ghrelin, which makes you hungry. Fat tissue releases leptin, which tells the brain "the stores are full".

once.soru: How does fat tissue send the "stores are full" message to the brain?

secenekler.neden: Fat tissue releases leptin, and leptin reaches the brain through the blood.
Fat tissue sends this message through the blood, not through nerves.
Fat tissue can also release hormones.

cards.p:
• Endocrine glands have no ducts. A hormone travels in the blood and affects its target cell.
• Hormonal effects start slowly, last long and affect a wide area.
• The hypothalamus and pituitary control the other glands. Negative feedback keeps the balance.
• Insulin and glucagon have opposite effects, and so do calcitonin and parathyroid hormone.

quiz.q: Match each hormone with where it is released.
quiz.e: Insulin is released by the β cells of the islets of Langerhans, and parathyroid hormone by the parathyroid glands. Cortisol comes from the cortex of the adrenal gland, and adrenaline from its medulla. Melatonin is the hormone of the pineal gland.

quiz.q: Group each hormone by its chemical structure.
quiz.e: Insulin, GH and ADH are proteins or peptides. Adrenaline, thyroxine and melatonin are amines derived from amino acids. Cortisol and aldosterone are steroids derived from cholesterol.

quiz.q: Put in order the chain that sets the cortisol level during long-lasting stress.
ogeler: The hypothalamus releases a releasing hormone
Cortisol puts the brakes on the hypothalamus and pituitary
quiz.e: This chain works on the same logic as the TRH-TSH-thyroxine chain. The hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary, and ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex. Rising cortisol puts the brakes on the chain. This is called negative feedback.

quiz.q: A healthy student's blood sugar rises above normal after lunch and returns to normal within two hours. What mainly brings it down?
o: Glucagon from the pancreas
Insulin from the pancreas
Adrenaline from the adrenal gland
Cortisol from the adrenal gland
quiz.e: When blood sugar rises, β cells release insulin. Cells take in glucose and the liver stores glycogen. Glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise blood sugar.
y: Glucagon raises blood sugar. The hormone that lowers sugar after a meal is insulin.
Adrenaline raises blood sugar. The hormone that lowers it by moving sugar into cells is insulin.
Cortisol raises blood sugar. The drop after a meal comes from insulin released by the pancreas.

duyu-organlari.title: Sense organs
duyu-organlari.summary: How do the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin detect stimuli?

cards.p: Light, sound, pressure or an odor molecule is a stimulus. A receptor picks up the stimulus and turns its energy into an electrical impulse. A sensory neuron then carries this impulse to the right sensory center in the brain.

cards.p: Receptors are grouped by the stimulus they detect. Mechanoreceptors detect touch and sound, thermoreceptors detect temperature, chemoreceptors detect taste and smell, and photoreceptors detect light. When the response to a lasting stimulus fades, this is called adaptation.

once.soru: You notice a smell when you enter a room. Why can't you smell it a few minutes later?

secenekler.neden: As the same stimulus continues, the receptor's response fades.
The odor molecules are still in the room. Someone who just walked in notices the smell right away.
The nose is clear. What changes is the receptor's response.

cards.p: The eye has three layers. The outer sclera becomes the clear cornea at the front. The middle choroid forms the iris at the front. The inner retina holds the receptors.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the eye and think about the path light takes.

noktalar.acik: The cornea is the clear front part of the sclera. It is the first structure to bend light.
The iris is the colored front part of the choroid. Its muscles narrow and widen the pupil.
The pupil is the opening in the middle of the iris. It controls how much light enters the eye.
The lens is flexible and clear. It focuses light onto the retina by changing its thickness.
The sclera is the tough outermost layer. It protects the eye and gives it its shape.
The retina is the innermost layer. Its rod and cone cells turn light into impulses.
The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain. Where the nerve leaves, there are no receptors. This is the blind spot.

cards.p: Eyebrows catch sweat, and eyelashes catch dust. The eyelids wipe the eye. The lacrimal gland keeps the eye moist, and the enzyme lysozyme in tears breaks down bacteria.

once.soru: Why does your nose run when you cry?

secenekler.neden: Extra tears drain into the nasal cavity through a duct at the inner corner of the eye.
The fluid running from the nose is mostly tears.
Breathing rate does not make the nose run.

cards.p: The lens is flexible, and its thickness is set by the ciliary muscles and the suspensory ligaments. When you look at something near, the lens gets thicker. When you look far away, it gets thinner. This is called accommodation.

cards.p: Rod cells in the retina are sensitive to dim light, but they do not tell colors apart. Cone cells detect colors and detail in bright light. There are three types of cones: red, green and blue.

once.soru: In moonlight you can see your surroundings, but you can hardly tell colors apart. Why?

secenekler.neden: In dim light, cones are not stimulated enough. Rods do not tell colors apart.
In dim light the pupil gets bigger.
The thickness of the lens affects focus, not color.

cards.h: The image, the fovea and the blind spot
cards.p: Light passes through the cornea, the pupil, the lens and the vitreous humor, in that order. An upside-down, smaller image forms on the retina. The sharpest image forms at the fovea, and no image forms at the blind spot.

once.soru: The image on your retina is upside down. So why do you see the world upright?

secenekler.neden: Perception happens in the brain, and the brain interprets the image as upright.
The lens does not fix the image. It makes it upside down.
The image on the retina really is upside down.

cards.p: In nearsightedness (myopia), the focus falls in front of the retina and faraway objects look blurry. A concave lens corrects it. In farsightedness (hyperopia), the focus falls behind the retina and nearby objects look blurry. A convex lens corrects it.

cards.p: In astigmatism, the curve of the cornea is uneven, and a cylindrical lens is used. In a cataract, the lens becomes cloudy. In color blindness, a defect in the cones usually makes red and green hard to tell apart.

once.soru: Color blindness comes from a defect in which retinal cells?

secenekler.neden: Three types of cones tell colors apart. If one of them is defective, some colors get mixed up.
Rods do not tell colors apart anyway.
Even with a healthy optic nerve, a defect in the cones causes color blindness.

cards.p: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. The hammer, anvil and stirrup bones amplify this vibration and pass it through the oval window to the cochlea. The organ of Corti in the cochlea turns the vibration into an impulse.

cards.key: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat. When your ears pop as you swallow on a plane, this tube is balancing the pressure.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the ear and follow the path of sound.

noktalar.acik: The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum. Its hairs and earwax trap dust.
The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates with sound waves. It separates the outer ear from the middle ear.
These ossicles are the smallest bones in the body. They amplify the eardrum's vibration and pass it to the inner ear.
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat. It balances the pressure on both sides of the eardrum.
The semicircular canals are three canals at right angles to each other. The fluid inside them lets us sense the head turning.
The hair cells of the organ of Corti inside the cochlea turn vibrations into impulses.
The auditory nerve carries impulses from the cochlea to the hearing center in the brain.

cards.p: The part of the cochlea near the entrance vibrates with high-pitched sounds, and the tip vibrates with low-pitched sounds. This is how the brain tells the pitch of a sound. As a sound gets louder, more hair cells are stimulated.

once.soru: A dog hears a dog whistle, but you don't. Why?

secenekler.neden: The human ear hears sounds between about 20 and 20,000 Hz. The whistle's sound is above this range.
The whistle's sound is strong. The issue is its frequency.

secenekler.yazi: Sound does not travel in air
secenekler.neden: Since the dog hears it, the sound must be traveling through the air.

cards.p: Balance is sensed in the inner ear. When the head turns, the fluid in the three semicircular canals moves. The ear stones in the utricle and saccule let us sense tilting and acceleration.

cards.p: Smell and taste are detected by chemoreceptors. Odor molecules dissolve in the mucus of the olfactory epithelium in the nose. The taste buds on the tongue are stimulated by substances dissolved in saliva.

cards.key: The "tongue map" is a myth. Every part of the tongue can detect all five tastes.

once.soru: Why can't you taste food well when you have a cold?

secenekler.neden: A blocked nose cannot pick up smells, and much of what we call taste comes from smell.
A cold does not kill taste buds.
The problem is in the nose, not the tongue.

cards.p: The skin is made of the epidermis, the dermis and a fat layer. The Malpighian layer of the epidermis divides and makes the pigment melanin. The dermis holds glands and receptors for touch, pressure, temperature and pain.

once.soru: Why does your skin get darker the longer you stay in the sun?

secenekler.neden: The Malpighian layer makes more melanin to protect against UV rays.
Redness comes from blood flow. Lasting darkening comes from melanin.
Skin color comes from the pigment melanin, not from dead cells.

cards.p: When the hair cells of the organ of Corti die, they are not replaced. So loud noise can cause permanent hearing loss. Smell and taste cells, on the other hand, are renewed. Protect your eyes from UV rays and your skin from the sun.

cards.key: If the people next to you can hear the music from your headphones, it is too loud. You should also have your eyes checked regularly.

once.soru: Are hair cells killed by loud noise replaced by new ones?

secenekler.neden: The hair cells of the organ of Corti are not renewed, so the loss is permanent.
Smell and taste cells are renewed, but hair cells are not.
Hair cells are never renewed.

cards.p:
• A receptor picks up the stimulus, a sensory neuron carries it to the brain, and perception happens in the brain.
• Rods work in dim light and cones handle color. The sharpest image forms at the fovea.
• Myopia is corrected with a concave lens and hyperopia with a convex lens.
• The cochlea handles hearing, and the semicircular canals handle balance.
• Smell and taste are detected by chemoreceptors.

quiz.q: Put in order the path a sound takes from the ear to the brain.
ogeler: Organ of Corti in the cochlea
quiz.e: Sound travels down the ear canal and makes the eardrum vibrate. The ossicles amplify the vibration and pass it to the inner ear. The hair cells of the organ of Corti turn the vibration into an impulse, and the auditory nerve carries the impulse to the brain. Perception happens in the brain.

quiz.q: Match each situation with the structure that detects it.
quiz.e: Rotation is detected by the semicircular canals, and linear acceleration by the ear stones in the utricle and saccule. Smell and taste are detected by chemoreceptors, and temperature by thermoreceptors in the skin.

quiz.q: Put each feature under the photoreceptor it belongs to.
quiz.e: Rods work in dim light and allow night vision, but they do not tell colors apart. Cones detect colors and detail in bright light. They come in three types, for red, green and blue, and are dense in the fovea.

quiz.q: Someone reading a book looks up through the window at a faraway tree. What changes in their eye?
o: Ciliary muscles contract, ligaments loosen, the lens thickens.
Ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tighten, the lens thins.
The iris contracts and thins the lens.
The ligaments loosen and the lens thins.
quiz.e: When looking far, the ciliary muscles relax and the suspensory ligaments tighten and pull on the lens. So the lens gets thinner and bends light less.
y: This happens when looking at something near. When you look far, the muscles relax and the lens gets thinner.
The iris only adjusts the pupil. The thickness of the lens is changed by the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments.
A loose ligament cannot pull on the lens. The lens gets thinner only when the ligaments tighten.

destek-hareket.title: Skeletal and muscular system
destek-hareket.summary: How does the skeleton carry us, and how do muscles contract?

cards.p: The skeleton supports the body, protects the organs and, together with the muscles, makes movement possible. Blood cells are made in red marrow. Bones also store calcium and phosphorus.

once.soru: What is the main job of the skull?

secenekler.neden: The skull is a hard box around the brain.
Blood cells are made in the red marrow inside bones.
The skull bones are joined by immovable joints and do not move.

cards.p: Cartilage is a flexible supporting tissue. Its cells, the chondrocytes, live in spaces in the matrix. Cartilage has no blood vessels, and nutrients arrive by diffusion. That is why cartilage heals slowly.

cards.key: The space where a cartilage cell sits is called a lacuna. Hyaline cartilage is found on joint surfaces and in the trachea, elastic cartilage in the outer ear, and fibrous cartilage in the discs between the vertebrae.

once.soru: Why does damaged cartilage in the knee heal so slowly?

secenekler.neden: Nutrients arrive slowly by diffusion, so repair is slow too.
Cartilage does have cells, the chondrocytes.
Cartilage is flexible. It heals slowly because it has no blood vessels.

cards.p: The shaft of a long bone is called the diaphysis, and it is made of compact bone. In its middle is the marrow cavity. The ends are called epiphyses, and they are made of spongy bone. The periosteum that covers the bone repairs fractures.

cards.key: Compact bone gives strength, and spongy bone keeps the bone light. The periosteum makes the bone thicker. The joint surfaces are covered with cartilage.

etk.soru: Tap the parts of the long bone.

noktalar.acik: Articular cartilage covers the ends of the bone. It reduces friction in the joint and cushions impact.
Spongy bone is the porous bone in the epiphysis. Its spaces hold red marrow, which makes blood cells.
As cartilage cells in the growth plate divide and turn into bone, the bone grows longer. This plate turns to bone at the end of puberty.
The periosteum is the membrane that covers the bone. It carries blood vessels and nerves, makes the bone thicker and repairs fractures.
Compact bone is the thick, hard wall of the diaphysis. It is made of Haversian systems.
The marrow cavity is in the middle of the diaphysis. In adults it is mostly filled with yellow marrow, which stores fat.

once.soru: Which structure repairs a broken bone?

secenekler.neden: The periosteum is the membrane that covers the bone. It carries blood vessels, nerves and bone-building cells.
Yellow marrow mostly stores fat.
Articular cartilage covers the ends of the bone and does not repair fractures.

cards.p: Red marrow makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Yellow marrow is mostly fat. With age, the marrow in the shafts of long bones turns yellow.

once.soru: What color is the marrow in a baby's long bones?

secenekler.neden: In babies almost all the marrow is red, and it turns yellow with age.
Yellow marrow forms with age.
Marrow is either red or yellow.

cards.p: Compact bone is made of Haversian systems, and the canal in the middle of each system holds blood vessels and nerves. Osteoblasts build bone and then become osteocytes. Osteoclasts break bone down.

once.soru: Is bone a living tissue that is constantly renewed?

secenekler.neden: Bone cells constantly build new bone and break down old bone.
Building and breakdown go on in bone throughout life.
Bone is constantly renewed in adults too.

cards.h: Types of bone and growth in length
cards.p: There are three kinds of bone: long bones like the thigh bone, short bones like the wrist bones and flat bones like the skull bones. A long bone grows longer as the cartilage in its growth plate divides and turns to bone.

cards.p: Skeletal muscle is striated and works under our control. Smooth muscle is not striated and works involuntarily. It is found in the walls of the stomach and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary, and its cells are linked by intercalated discs.

cards.p: Skeletal muscle is made of long muscle fibers, each fiber is made of myofibrils, and each myofibril is made of sarcomeres. The regular arrangement of thin actin and thick myosin filaments makes the muscle look striated.

once.soru: What makes muscle look striated under a microscope?

secenekler.neden: When thick and thin filaments line up regularly, light and dark bands form.
Nuclei do not form the stripes.
Blood vessels do not form regular bands.

cards.p: During contraction the filaments do not shorten. They slide past each other. Acetylcholine stimulates the muscle membrane, and Ca²⁺ ions are released. This opens the binding sites on actin. Then the myosin heads pull on actin using the energy of ATP.

cards.p: Muscle contracts only with ATP, and the ready supply of ATP lasts a few seconds. Creatine phosphate quickly renews ATP. After that comes aerobic respiration, and if there is not enough oxygen, lactic acid fermentation.

cards.p: A single stimulus causes a brief contraction. This is called a twitch. If stimuli come one after another, the contractions add up and the muscle stays contracted without a break. This is called tetanus. When ATP runs low, the muscle's force drops. This is called fatigue.

once.soru: What happens if you stimulate a muscle again and again without letting it relax?

secenekler.neden: The contractions pile up and the muscle contracts without a break.
For the muscle to relax, the stimuli have to stop.
Separate twitches need time to relax between stimuli.

cards.h: Types of contraction and the motor unit
cards.p: A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it stimulates are called a motor unit. If many units are stimulated, the muscle contracts strongly. In an isotonic contraction the muscle shortens, and in an isometric contraction its length does not change.

once.soru: You push a wall with all your strength, and it does not move. Are your muscles contracting?

secenekler.neden: The muscle tenses and uses ATP, but its length does not change.
If your muscles were not contracting, you could not push at all.
Because the wall does not move, the length of your arm does not change.

cards.p: Muscles can only pull, not push. That is why there are antagonistic pairs of muscles that work against each other. For example, when the biceps contracts the arm bends and the triceps relaxes. The slight tension in a resting muscle is called muscle tone.

once.soru: Why might the bones of a child who never sees the sun become soft?

secenekler.neden: Vitamin D is made in the skin with sunlight and is needed to absorb calcium.
What softens bone is a lack of calcium.
Marrow makes blood cells and does not decide how hard the bone is.

cards.p:
• The skeleton supports and protects the body. Blood cells are made in the marrow.
• Osteoblasts build bone, and osteoclasts break it down.
• A long bone grows from its growth plate. Joints are immovable, slightly movable or movable.
• Skeletal muscle is voluntary, while smooth and cardiac muscle are involuntary.
• In contraction, actin slides, and Ca²⁺ and ATP are needed.

quiz.q: Match each cell with its job.
ciftler: Bone cell embedded in the matrix
Cartilage cell living in a lacuna
quiz.e: An osteoblast builds bone and becomes an osteocyte once it is embedded in the matrix. An osteoclast breaks bone down. A chondrocyte is the cartilage cell that lives in a lacuna.

quiz.q: Put the events of a skeletal muscle contraction in order.
ogeler: Ca²⁺ binds to troponin and tropomyosin shifts
Using ATP's energy, actin is pulled toward the middle of the sarcomere
quiz.e: Acetylcholine released by the motor neuron stimulates the muscle membrane. When the signal reaches the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca²⁺ is released. When Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, tropomyosin shifts and the binding sites open. The myosin heads attach to actin and pull it using ATP.

quiz.q: When a muscle contracts, what happens to the length of each structure?
quiz.e: The filaments do not shorten. They slide past each other. So actin, myosin and the A band, which is as long as myosin, keep their length. As actin slides to the middle, the sarcomere, the I band and the H zone get shorter.

quiz.q: A 15-year-old student's X-ray shows that the growth plate at the end of the femur is still open, so cartilage is visible. In their 25-year-old sister, this plate has turned to bone. What can be concluded?
o: Neither of them can grow taller anymore.
The sister keeps growing taller thanks to the periosteum.
Bone gets thicker only through the growth plate.
The student's long bones can still grow longer.
quiz.e: The bone grows longer as the cartilage in the growth plate divides. Once the plate turns to bone, growth in length stops. The bone gets thicker thanks to the periosteum.
y: The student's growth plate is still cartilage. So their bones can still grow longer.
The periosteum makes bone thicker, not longer. The sister, whose plate has turned to bone, can no longer grow taller.
The growth plate is for growth in length. Thickening happens thanks to the periosteum.

sindirim.title: Digestive system
sindirim.summary: How is food broken down, where is it digested, and how does it reach the blood?

cards.p: Digestion is the breaking of large food molecules into small units that can cross membranes. Mechanical digestion makes food physically smaller. In chemical digestion, enzymes break bonds by hydrolysis.

once.soru: Why can't the starch we eat go straight into the blood?

secenekler.neden: Starch is made of thousands of glucose units. It must first be split into glucose to cross a membrane.
Starch does not disappear in the stomach. Its digestion is completed in the small intestine.
Starch is an important source of energy.

cards.h: The digestive tract and accessory organs
cards.p: Food moves through a one-way tube. This tube is made of the mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus, in that order. Accessory organs release their secretions into this tube.

etk.soru: Put in order the path food takes through the digestive tract.

cards.p: Teeth grind food, and this mechanical digestion increases the surface area. Saliva makes the bite slippery and contains salivary amylase. That is why the chemical digestion of starch starts in the mouth.

cards.p: When you swallow, the epiglottis closes the windpipe. The esophagus does not release enzymes. The bite is pushed to the stomach by wave-like contractions of ring-shaped muscles. This movement is called peristalsis.

cards.key: If food goes down the windpipe, you cough. Peristalsis happens all the way from the esophagus to the anus.

once.soru: Can you drink water while upside down?

secenekler.neden: The bite is moved by the muscles of the esophagus, not by gravity.
The esophagus can push liquid upward too, with waves of muscle.
What matters here is muscle movement, not speed.

cards.p: The stomach releases HCl, and the pH inside drops to about 2. HCl turns pepsinogen into pepsin, so protein digestion starts in the stomach. Mucus protects the stomach wall from the acid.

cards.key: Stomach acid kills most microbes. Chyme passes little by little through the pylorus into the small intestine. No nutrients are absorbed in the stomach.

once.soru: The stomach releases such strong acid. Why doesn't it digest itself?

secenekler.neden: The mucus lining the stomach wall keeps acid and pepsin away from it.
The acid is in the stomach cavity. Without protection it would damage the wall.
If the mucus breaks down, the stomach wall is digested and an ulcer forms.

cards.p: The first part of the small intestine is called the duodenum. The bicarbonate in pancreatic juice neutralizes the acid coming from the stomach. Of the pancreatic enzymes, amylase digests starch, trypsin digests protein and lipase digests fat.

cards.p: Protein-digesting enzymes are released as inactive precursors so they do not digest the cells that make them. In the stomach, HCl activates pepsinogen. In the duodenum, enterokinase activates trypsinogen, and trypsin then activates the other enzymes.

once.soru: Why does the pancreas release trypsin in an inactive form (trypsinogen)?

secenekler.neden: Active trypsin would also break down the proteins of the pancreatic cells that make it.
An inactive enzyme does not work. It has to be activated first.

secenekler.yazi: So it travels in the blood
secenekler.neden: Trypsinogen is sent to the intestine through a duct, not into the blood.

cards.h: The liver, bile and the gallbladder
cards.p: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder. Bile is not an enzyme. It breaks fat into tiny droplets, which is called emulsification. This increases the surface where lipase can work.

cards.p: Maltase, sucrase and lactase in the lining of the small intestine split disaccharides. Peptidases split short peptides into amino acids. The chemical digestion of all foods is completed in the small intestine.

once.soru: Which enzyme breaks down lactose, the sugar in milk?

secenekler.neden: Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
Lipase breaks down fats.
Pepsin breaks down proteins.

cards.p: Chemical digestion starts in the mouth for carbohydrates, in the stomach for proteins and in the small intestine for fats. All of them finish in the small intestine. Vitamins, minerals and water are absorbed without being digested.

cards.p: Villi and microvilli greatly increase the absorbing surface. Glucose and amino acids pass into the capillary blood and travel to the liver through the hepatic portal vein. Most fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lymph.

cards.p: The large intestine does not release enzymes. It absorbs the remaining water and minerals and turns the leftovers into feces. The helpful bacteria living there make vitamin K and some B vitamins.

once.soru: Why does the body lose water quickly with diarrhea?

secenekler.yazi: The large intestine can't absorb water
secenekler.neden: The leftovers pass through the large intestine too quickly. So the water is expelled before it can be absorbed.
The stomach releases acid and enzymes. The main place of water loss is the large intestine.
With diarrhea, gut movement does not stop. It speeds up.

cards.p: Seeing or smelling food starts secretion through nerves. Gastrin increases gastric juice. Secretin makes the pancreas release bicarbonate. Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder and empties the bile.

once.soru: What makes your mouth water when you smell food?

secenekler.neden: The smell reaches the brain, and the brain stimulates the salivary glands through nerves.
There is no food in the stomach yet, so hormones have not stepped in.
The pancreas does not control saliva.

cards.p: A sore that opens in the stomach when the mucus breaks down is called an ulcer. When stomach contents flow back into the esophagus, it is called reflux. People with lactose intolerance have little lactase. High-fiber foods prevent constipation.

once.soru: Is the cellulose (fiber) we can't digest wasted?

secenekler.yazi: No, it keeps the gut moving
secenekler.neden: Fiber increases gut movement and prevents constipation.
Even though cellulose is not digested, it helps gut movement.
Cellulose is not digested, so it is not absorbed.

cards.p:
• Mechanical digestion breaks food apart, and in chemical digestion enzymes carry out hydrolysis.
• Carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth, protein in the stomach and fat in the small intestine. All of them finish in the small intestine.
• Bile is not an enzyme. It emulsifies fat.
• Glucose and amino acids pass from the villi into the blood, and fats into the lymph. The large intestine absorbs water.

quiz.q: Put each enzyme under the food group it digests.
quiz.e: Amylase breaks down starch, and maltase and lactase break down disaccharides. Pepsin, trypsin and peptidases digest proteins, and lipase digests fats.

quiz.q: Put in order what happens to a protein until it is digested and absorbed.
ogeler: In the stomach, HCl turns pepsinogen into pepsin
Pepsin splits the protein into short polypeptides
Peptidases split short peptides into amino acids
Amino acids pass into the capillary blood of the villus
quiz.e: Protein digestion starts in the stomach with pepsin. In the duodenum, enterokinase activates trypsin, and trypsin activates chymotrypsin. Peptidases on the microvillus membrane take the last step, and the amino acids are absorbed into the blood.

quiz.q: Match each secretion with its job.
quiz.e: Gastrin increases gastric juice, and secretin increases the pancreas's bicarbonate release. Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder. Bile emulsifies fat, and bicarbonate neutralizes the acid of the chyme.

quiz.q: Someone has had their gallbladder removed by surgery. What becomes hardest for them?
o: Digesting fats after a fatty meal
Digesting starch in the mouth
Digesting proteins in the stomach
Absorbing water in the large intestine
quiz.e: The liver keeps making bile, but it cannot be stored. So after a fatty meal, not enough bile arrives at once and fat digestion becomes harder.
y: Starch digestion in the mouth is done by salivary amylase. Bile only plays a role in emulsifying fats.
Protein digestion in the stomach is done by pepsin and HCl. Bile emulsifies fats.
Water absorption in the large intestine does not depend on bile. Bile helps digest fats.

dolasim-bagisiklik.title: Circulatory and immune systems
dolasim-bagisiklik.summary: The heart, blood vessels, blood, lymph and the body's lines of defense.

cards.p: The heart is a pump made of cardiac muscle. It has two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom. Valves keep blood flowing in one direction. There is a tricuspid valve on the right side and a bicuspid valve on the left.

cards.p: The heart makes its own signal to contract. The SA node starts the signal, and the AV node holds it briefly and passes it to the ventricles. Contraction is called systole, and relaxing and filling with blood is called diastole. One cycle takes about 0.8 seconds.

cards.p: In pulmonary circulation, blood goes from the right ventricle to the lungs, picks up oxygen and returns to the left atrium. In systemic circulation, blood goes from the left ventricle through the aorta to the tissues, drops off its oxygen and returns to the right atrium.

cards.h: Blood vessels, pulse and blood pressure
cards.p: An artery carries blood away from the heart. Its elastic wall stretches with every beat, and this stretch is called the pulse. A vein brings blood back to the heart, has low pressure and has valves. The wall of a capillary is one cell thick.
cards.key: Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg. The larger number shows systole, and the smaller number shows diastole. The muscles around the veins push the blood in them toward the heart.

once.soru: Which vessel do you count your pulse from at your wrist?

secenekler.neden: The artery wall stretches with every beat. You feel this wave with your finger.
The pressure in a vein is low, so no pulse can be felt.
Capillaries are so thin that no pulse can be taken from them.

cards.p: Blood flows slowest in the capillaries. At the arterial end of a capillary, blood pressure wins, so water and small molecules filter into the tissue. At the venous end, osmotic pressure pulls the water back.

once.soru: When your throat is infected, why do the glands under your jaw swell?

secenekler.neden: Lymph nodes filter out microbes. Lymphocytes multiply there and the node swells.
The swollen structures are lymph nodes, not blood vessels.
The swollen glands are lymph nodes, not salivary glands.

cards.p: About 55% of blood is plasma. Plasma holds water, proteins, ions and nutrients. Red blood cells carry oxygen with hemoglobin, white blood cells defend the body, and platelets start clotting.

cards.p: At a wound, platelets form a plug and release thromboplastin. With the help of Ca2+, thromboplastin turns prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin, and the fibrin mesh forms the clot.

once.soru: Why does blood clot at a wound and not inside the vessel?

secenekler.neden: Thromboplastin is released from injured tissue and platelets.
Ca²⁺ is always present in blood.
Fibrinogen is always present in plasma, but it does not turn into fibrin without a wound.

cards.p: Blood type is set by the antigens on the membrane of red blood cells. Plasma holds antibodies against the antigens the person lacks. If the donor's antigen meets the recipient's antibody, the red blood cells clump.

once.soru: A person's blood clumps only in anti-B serum. What is their blood type?

secenekler.neden: Clumping in anti-B serum shows the B antigen. There is no clumping in anti-D serum, so the person is Rh−.
If the person were type A, there would be clumping in anti-A serum, and if Rh+, in anti-D serum.
If the person were type AB, there would also be clumping in anti-A serum.

cards.p: Innate defense gives the same response to every microbe. The first line of defense is the skin, mucus and stomach acid. The second line includes phagocytosis, inflammation and fever.

once.soru: Why does a small cut on your hand turn red and swell?

secenekler.neden: The blood vessels widen and more blood and defense cells reach the area.
A clot stops bleeding. The redness and swelling come from inflammation.
The first response at a cut comes from innate defense, not antibodies.

cards.p: A macrophage displays a piece of the microbe on its surface, and a helper T cell recognizes this piece. B lymphocytes release antibodies, which is called humoral immunity. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells, which is called cell-mediated immunity. In the end, memory cells remain.

once.soru: Which cell directly kills a cell that a virus has entered?

secenekler.neden: A cytotoxic T cell recognizes the infected cell and destroys it directly. This is called cell-mediated immunity.
A B lymphocyte makes antibodies, but it does not kill the cell directly.
A red blood cell carries oxygen. It does not defend the body.

cards.p: In active immunity, the body makes the antibodies itself. It starts late but lasts long, and it is gained by having a disease or getting a vaccine. In passive immunity, ready-made antibodies are received. Antiserum and breast milk protect this way, and the effect starts right away but does not last long.

once.soru: Who could be the best donor for a kidney transplant?

secenekler.neden: Tissue antigens are inherited and are the same in identical twins.
Tissue antigens vary a lot from person to person.

secenekler.yazi: Anyone with the same blood type
secenekler.neden: A matching blood type is not enough. Tissue antigens are checked too.

cards.p: An overreaction to a harmless substance is called an allergy. When the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, it is called an autoimmune disease. In AIDS, the HIV virus destroys helper T cells. A drop in hemoglobin in the blood is called anemia.

once.soru: In a pollen allergy, which substance causes the itching and swelling?

secenekler.neden: Mast cells release histamine. The vessels widen and itching starts.
Insulin regulates blood sugar.
Hemoglobin carries O₂.

cards.p:
• The heart has four chambers, and the SA node starts the signal to contract.
• Pulmonary circulation oxygenates blood in the lungs, and systemic circulation delivers it to the tissues.
• In clotting, thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin.
• If a serum causes clumping, the red cells carry that antigen.
• Active immunity lasts, while passive immunity is fast but short-lived.

quiz.q: After a run, a person's pulse is 120 beats/min. How many seconds does one heart cycle take?
quiz.e: One minute is 60 seconds. 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 seconds. When the heart speeds up, the cycle gets shorter, and diastole shortens the most.

quiz.q: Match the serum results (+ clumping, − no clumping) with the blood type.
quiz.e: A serum with clumping shows that the red cells carry that antigen. Clumping in anti-A shows A, in anti-B shows B, and in anti-D shows the Rh (D) antigen. If there is no clumping in either anti-A or anti-B, the blood type is O.

quiz.q: Group each case by the type of immunity.
quiz.e: In active immunity, the body makes the antibodies itself. Getting a vaccine and having the disease are examples. In passive immunity, ready-made antibodies are received. Antiserum, antibodies from the mother through the placenta and milk, and the anti-D shot are examples.

quiz.q: Someone who has taken antibiotics for a long time has fewer gut bacteria and now lacks vitamin K. Which step of clotting is directly affected?
o: Platelets sticking to the wound
Making prothrombin
The fibrin mesh trapping cells
Absorbing Ca²⁺ ions from the intestine
quiz.e: The liver makes prothrombin using vitamin K. When prothrombin drops, less thrombin and therefore less fibrin form, and bleeding lasts longer.
y: Platelets do not depend on vitamin K. The plug forms, but the clot sets late.
The fibrin mesh is a later step. The real problem is that there is less thrombin to make fibrin.
Ca²⁺ absorption is increased by vitamin D, not vitamin K.

solunum.title: Respiratory system
solunum.summary: How does air get in, and how are gases exchanged and carried?

cards.h: What does the respiratory system do?
cards.p: The respiratory system carries out gas exchange. It passes O2 from the air into the blood and removes CO2 from the blood. Every cell makes its own ATP through cellular respiration.

once.soru: What is the main job of the respiratory system?

secenekler.neden: The respiratory system passes O₂ into the blood and removes CO₂.
Every cell makes its own ATP through cellular respiration.
The heart pumps blood.

cards.h: The path of air: from nose to alveolus
cards.p: Air passes through the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles, in that order, to reach the alveoli. When you swallow, the epiglottis closes the larynx.

etk.soru: Put in order the path the air you breathe takes to the alveolus.

cards.p: The capillaries in the airways warm the air, and the moist surface moistens it. Hairs and mucus filter out dust. Cilia sweep the mucus toward the pharynx.

once.soru: In winter you breathe cold air through your nose. How does the air reach the alveoli?

secenekler.neden: The capillaries and moist surface of the nose and airways prepare the air.
The airways warm and moisten the air before it reaches the alveoli.
Besides filtering, the airways also warm and moisten the air.

cards.p: The right lung has 3 lobes and the left lung has 2, because the left side makes room for the heart. The two-layered pleura around the lung and the fluid between its layers reduce friction.

once.soru: Can the lungs expand with their own muscles?

secenekler.neden: The lungs have no skeletal muscle. Muscles expand the chest, and the lungs follow.
The lungs cannot contract and relax on their own.
Even in a deep breath, it is the chest and abdominal muscles that expand the chest.

cards.p: When you breathe in, the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles contract. The chest volume increases, the pressure drops below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. At rest, breathing out happens passively.

cards.p: In a calm breath, about 500 mL of air moves in and out, and this is called the tidal volume. The tidal volume plus the reserve volumes is called the vital capacity, which is about 4600 mL. 1200 mL of residual air always stays in the lungs.

cards.key: With effort you can breathe in 3000 mL more and breathe out 1100 mL more. Residual air is not part of the vital capacity.

once.soru: Sitting calmly, about how much air do you take in with one breath?

secenekler.neden: A calm breath is about 500 mL.
That is close to the deepest breath possible. A calm breath takes in much less air.
That is far too little, only about a sip of water.

cards.h: The alveolus: the gas exchange surface
cards.p: Hundreds of millions of alveoli have a total surface of about 70 m2, and their walls are one cell thick. O2 passes into the blood and CO2 into the alveolus by diffusion, driven by partial pressure differences.

cards.key: No ATP is used in this exchange. Surfactant lowers surface tension, so the alveoli do not collapse and stick together.

cards.p: Cells in the tissues use O<sub>2</sub> and make CO<sub>2</sub>. So in the tissue, PO<sub>2</sub> is low and PCO<sub>2</sub> is high. O<sub>2</sub> passes from the blood to the cells, and CO<sub>2</sub> from the cells to the blood.

cards.key: In the alveolus, O₂ enters the blood, and in the tissue it leaves the blood. Partial pressure decides which way a gas moves.

once.soru: Blood from the lungs has a PO₂ of 100, and a working muscle has 20 mmHg. Where does O₂ go?

secenekler.neden: A gas diffuses from where its partial pressure is high to where it is low.
PO₂ is lower in the muscle, so O₂ goes there.
As long as there is a pressure difference, diffusion continues.

cards.p: About 98.5% of O2 is carried bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells. When PO2 is low, CO2 is high, or the surroundings are warm or acidic, hemoglobin releases O2 easily.

cards.key: One hemoglobin binds 4 molecules of O₂. Fetal hemoglobin binds O₂ more tightly and takes O₂ from the mother's blood in the placenta.

cards.p: About 70% of CO2 is carried in plasma as bicarbonate (HCO3−). The enzyme carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells quickly combines CO2 with water.
